title: The Determinant of a Square Matrix

blocks.title: Determinant of a 2×2 Matrix
teacherCues: Write the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ and ask: How do we compute $ad - bc$?
Show that if the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular (no inverse).

discoveryHook.scenario: The determinant tells you if a matrix is invertible, just like checking if a number is zero before dividing. For a 2×2 matrix, it's simply the product of the main diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal.

explanation: The [[kw:determinant]] of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is the number $ \det(A) = |A| = ad - bc $.
It can be positive, negative, or zero. If $\det(A) = 0$, then $A$ is singular (not invertible).
The determinant is calculated by multiplying the main diagonal entries and subtracting the product of the off-diagonal entries.

formulaCard.title: Determinant of a 2×2 Matrix
formulaCard.formula: $$\det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc$$
notes: If $ad - bc = 0$, the matrix has no inverse.

examples.title: B – When is it zero?
examples.prompt: For what value of $k$ is the determinant of $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & k \\ 6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ equal to zero?
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to your partner: set up $ad-bc=0$, plug in, and solve for $k$.
steps: So when $k=1$, the determinant is zero, and the matrix is singular.

confusionCorner.title: Don't mix up the order
confusionCorner.body: It's always $ad - bc$, not $bc - ad$. The product of the main diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal.

questions.prompt: The determinant of $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is $ad$ minus ___.
hints: The product of the other diagonal.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$? (Enter a number)
If the determinant of a matrix is zero, the matrix is called ___.

blocks.title: Minors and Cofactors
teacherCues: Write a 3×3 matrix. Show how to delete a row and column to form a 2×2 determinant (the minor).
Then multiply by $(-1)^{i+j}$ to get the cofactor. Display the checkerboard sign pattern.

discoveryHook.scenario: To find the determinant of a larger matrix, we break it down into smaller 2×2 pieces called minors, then adjust their signs with a checkerboard pattern. This process, called cofactor expansion, unlocks the determinant of any size.

explanation: For a square matrix, the [[kw:minor]] $M_{ij}$ is the determinant of the submatrix formed by deleting row $i$ and column $j$.
The [[kw:cofactor]] $C_{ij}$ is $(-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$, which adjusts the sign according to a checkerboard pattern (positive for even $i+j$, negative for odd).
These cofactors are the building blocks for finding determinants of matrices $3\times3$ or larger.

formulaCard.title: Cofactor Formula
notes: $M_{ij}$: determinant of matrix without row $i$, column $j$.
Sign: positive if $i+j$ is even, negative if odd.

examples.title: A – Find a minor and cofactor
B – Find $C_{12}$
examples.prompt: Using the same matrix, find the cofactor $C_{12}$.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to your partner: delete the first row and second column. Compute the 2×2 determinant, then apply the sign from the checkerboard.

confusionCorner.title: Sign errors are common
confusionCorner.body: Remember the checkerboard: position (1,1) is +, (1,2) is -, (1,3) is +, etc. For $C_{ij}$, multiply the minor by $(-1)^{i+j}$.

questions.prompt: The minor $M_{ij}$ is the determinant of the matrix after deleting row $i$ and column ___.
In the sign pattern for cofactors, what is the sign for $C_{23}$? (+ or -)

hints: It's the determinant of the smaller matrix.

blocks.title: Determinant of 3×3 and Higher
teacherCues: Write a 3×3 matrix and show expansion by cofactors along the first row: $a_{11}C_{11} + a_{12}C_{12} + a_{13}C_{13}$.
Emphasize that any row or column can be used, but picking one with zeros simplifies the work.

discoveryHook.scenario: Expanding by cofactors is like systematically reducing a large matrix into many 2×2 determinants. By choosing a row or column with zeros, many terms vanish, making the calculation much faster.

explanation: The determinant of an $n \times n$ matrix (for $n \ge 2$) is the sum of the entries in any row (or column) multiplied by their cofactors: $\det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} C_{ij}$ (expansion along row $i$).
For a $3 \times 3$ matrix, expanding along the first row gives $a_{11}C_{11} + a_{12}C_{12} + a_{13}C_{13}$.
This works for any size; each cofactor involves a determinant one size smaller.

formulaCard.title: Cofactor Expansion
formulaCard.formula: $$\det(A) = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + \cdots + a_{in}C_{in}$$ for any row $i$.
notes: Choose the row or column with the most zeros to simplify.

examples.title: A – 3×3 determinant by first row
examples.prompt: Find $\det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ using cofactor expansion along the first row.

examples.title: B – Expand along a different row
examples.prompt: Using the same matrix, expand along the second row to verify the determinant is $-3$.
examples.peerPrompt: Work with your partner: compute the three cofactors for row 2, then multiply by the entries and sum.

examples.title: C – Verify with first column
examples.prompt: Expand along the first column of the same matrix and confirm you still get $-3$.

confusionCorner.title: Check your signs
confusionCorner.body: The most common mistake is forgetting the minus signs in cofactors. Use the checkerboard pattern: top-left is +, then alternate.

questions.prompt: Expanding by cofactors means multiplying each entry of a row by its cofactor and then taking the ___.
In the expansion along the first row of the example matrix, what was the cofactor $C_{12}$? (Enter a number)
hints: It was the cofactor of the entry $0$.

questions.prompt: To minimize work, expand along the row or column with the most ___.
hints: Entries that are zero make the term vanish.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Choose the row or column with the most zeros.

blocks.title: Using Zeros to Simplify
teacherCues: Show a 4×4 matrix with a column of zeros. Ask: Which column would you expand along? Why?
Demonstrate that only one cofactor needs to be computed because the others are multiplied by zero.

discoveryHook.scenario: A 4×4 matrix looks intimidating, but if you spot a column with three zeros, the determinant reduces to just one 3×3 determinant—saving a ton of work. Smart expansion is the key.

explanation: When a row or column has many zeros, expanding along that row/column simplifies the calculation dramatically.
For each zero entry, the term $a_{ij}C_{ij}$ is zero, so you only need to compute cofactors for the nonzero entries.
This works for any size matrix; just pick the row or column with the fewest nonzeros.

formulaCard.title: Smart Expansion
formulaCard.formula: If a column has only one nonzero entry $a_{ij}$, then $\det(A) = a_{ij} C_{ij}$ (no sum needed).
notes: Always look for rows or columns with many zeros.
The cofactor $C_{ij}$ itself may be expanded similarly.

examples.title: A – 4×4 with a column of zeros
steps: $M_{13}$ is the determinant of the submatrix after removing row 1 and column 3: $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
Expand that 3×3 along row 2 (zeros? row2 has 0,2,3): $0\cdot C_{21} + 2\cdot C_{22} + 3\cdot C_{23}$.

examples.title: B – Why choose that column?
examples.prompt: Explain why expanding along column 3 was the smart choice.
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss: How many zero entries are in column 3? How many terms do we actually compute?
steps: Only the first entry is nonzero, so we only need its cofactor $C_{13}$.
The other three terms are zero, saving us from computing three 3×3 determinants.

examples.title: C – Find determinant of a 3×3 with zeros
examples.prompt: Use expansion along a row/column with zeros: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.
steps: Expand along first row (two zeros): $2 \cdot C_{11}$. $C_{11} = \det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} = 18$.

confusionCorner.title: Don't forget the sign on the cofactor
confusionCorner.body: Even when expanding along a column with only one nonzero, you must still multiply by $(-1)^{i+j}$. For $C_{13}$, the sign is positive because $1+3=4$ (even).

questions.prompt: When a column has only one nonzero entry $a_{ij}$, the determinant simplifies to $a_{ij}$ times its ___.
In the 4×4 example, what was the value of the determinant? (Enter a number)
Expanding along a row or column with many zeros ___ the number of calculations.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Determinant of a 3×3 via First Row
teacherCues: Pose: Find the determinant of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ using cofactor expansion along the first row.
Outline Understand (identify row, compute cofactors), Solve (compute each cofactor, multiply and sum), Conclude (state determinant).

discoveryHook.scenario: By following a systematic blueprint—choose a row, compute the three cofactors, and add the products—you can find the determinant of any 3×3 matrix accurately.

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Choose the first row: $a_{11}=1$, $a_{12}=3$, $a_{13}=-2$. Compute their cofactors $C_{11}$, $C_{12}$, $C_{13}$.

examples.title: A – Understand the setup
examples.prompt: Write the first row entries and the corresponding checkerboard signs.

examples.title: B – Compute cofactors
examples.prompt: Work with a partner to find $C_{11}$, $C_{12}$, $C_{13}$.
examples.peerPrompt: For each, delete the first row and the column, compute the 2×2 determinant, then apply the sign.

examples.title: C – Conclude
examples.prompt: Sum the products to get the determinant.

confusionCorner.title: Sign of the middle entry
confusionCorner.body: Remember that for position (1,2), the sign is negative. So $C_{12} = -M_{12}$.

questions.prompt: In the blueprint, the cofactor $C_{11}$ had a ___ sign.
What was the determinant of the blueprint matrix? (Enter a number)
Expanding along the first row requires computing ___ cofactors for a $3 \times 3$ matrix.

challengeCorner.prompt: Find the determinant of $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ by expanding along a row/column with zeros. (Hint: choose row 2 or column 3 for lots of zeros.)
hints: Expand along row 2: only $a_{22}=3$ is nonzero, so det = $3 C_{22}$.
Compute $C_{22}$ from the submatrix, then multiply.
